{{Short description|Transcendental plane curve}}
{{Distinguish|Butterfly curve (algebraic)}}
[[Image:Animated construction of butterfly curve.gif|thumb|The butterfly curve with animated construction gives an idea of the complexity of the [[curve]].]]
The '''butterfly curve''' is a [[Transcendental function|transcendental]] [[plane curve]] discovered by Temple H. Fay of [[University of Southern Mississippi]] in 1989.<ref name="origin">{{cite journal
 | last = Fay | first = Temple H.
 | date = May 1989
 | title = The Butterfly Curve
 | journal = Amer. Math. Monthly
 | volume = 96 | issue = 5 | pages = 442–443
 | doi = 10.2307/2325155
 | jstor=2325155
}}</ref>  

==Equation==
For <math> 0 \le t \le 12\pi </math>, the curve is given by the following [[parametric equation]]s:<ref>{{MathWorld|title=Butterfly Curve|urlname=ButterflyCurve}}</ref>
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
 x &= \sin t \!\left(e^{\cos t} - 2\cos 4t - \sin^5 \left(\frac{t}{12}\right)\right) \\
 y &= \cos t \!\left(e^{\cos t} - 2\cos 4t - \sin^5 \left(\frac{t}{12}\right)\right)
\end{align}
</math>
or by the following [[polar equation]]:
<math display="block"> r = e^{\sin\theta} - 2\cos \left(4\theta\right) + \sin^5\left(\frac{2\theta - \pi}{24}\right).</math>

The {{math|sin}} term has been added for purely aesthetic reasons, to make the butterfly appear fuller and more pleasing to the eye.<ref name="origin" />

== Developments ==
In 2006, two mathematicians using [[Mathematica]] analyzed the function and found variants where leaves, flowers, or other insects became apparent.<ref>{{cite journal|date=June 2008| title = On the analysis and construction of the butterfly curve using Mathematica| journal =  International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology | volume = 39| issue = 5| pages = 670–678| doi = 10.1080/00207390801923240| last1 = Geum| first1 = Y.H.| last2 = Kim| first2 = Y.I.| s2cid = 122066238}}</ref> New developments regarding such curves are still under research by mathematicians.
